every person refusing to take the oath of allegiance and supremacy, and to receive sacrament after the form of the Church of England. should be held incapable of any public employment, civil or military. It was forther required that no person should hold any such otlice without repudiating the doctrine of transubs.antiation. This Act was expreasly meant to affect injuriously the Roman Catholics, but it applied with equal I force to the Nonconformists. The latter I agreed to it because they were solemnly promised that a relief bill would be intro- duced to exempt them from its operation; "but," as Sir Erskine May observes, " the Church party, having secured them in its toils, SIM in no hurry to release them." So from 1673 to 1828, a law excluding Proteetant Dissenters from all civil or military offices, except on the condition of occasional confor- mity, remained on our statute book. One by one the oppressive Acts were re- laxed, and finally repealed ; the Corporation , and Teat Acts alone (we exclude the Ant of Uniformity) remaining. Various attempts I were made to repeal them also. The city of London had raised no less than 215 000 in Sacs by electing Dissenters to offices of trust, which under the provisions of the Cor- poration Act they could not accept. The exaction become as intolerable as it was shameful, but the Corporation persevered, and brought the cam for ju .gment in the House of Lords. The (Whig) Chaneellor Mansfield defended the resistance of the Dissenters, and in condemning the laws to force oonscience said—" There in nothing certainly more unreasonable, more inconsis- tent with the rights of human nature, more contrary to the spirit and precepts of the Christian religion, more iniquitous and un- just, more impolitio, than peraeoution. Ills against natural religion, revealed religion, and sound policy." In 1787 Mr. Holiday brought forward a motion to abolish the Acts. Pitt seemed disposed to support him, but yielded to the opinions of the bishops while Lord North, as a good Tory, regarded the Teets Act "as the great bulwark of the constitution, to winch we owed these Meatimable blessings of freedom, which we now happily enjoyed." The mamas) was defeated by • small majority; but was brought forward next year. Pox strongly supported the motion. and then used words which should here. membered in a coming and greater struggle, , He said—. It would perhaps bd contended that the repeal of the Corporation and Test Acts might enable the Dissenters to obtain • majority. This he scarcely thought pro- bable ; but it appeared fully sufficient to answer, that if the majority of the people of England should ever be for the abolition of , the Established Church, in such a ease the abolition should immediately follow." The French Revolution and the war as rested program in this, se in other directions, and it remained for Lord John Russell, in 1828. to have the honour of bringiug the subject before the House.
